chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. A question about the class gives a list, counting turns the list into a table, and the table is then shown as a pictograph and as a bar graph, with the scale as the idea that ties the pictures to the numbers.

points.title: Ask a question, then collect
points.text: Every graph starts from a question such as which game is most popular, so the data is collected, counted and ordered before it is drawn.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's examples, a tool only where handling the data is the idea, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.

points.title: The scale tells the story
points.text: A symbol or a unit of bar length always stands for a number. Reading and drawing both start by finding that number.

points.title: Keeko's doubts
points.text: The common wrong ideas, such as 'the longest list entry is the most popular' or 'a bar of 6 units is always 6', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a count or a scale, never just a rule.

concepts.concept_name: A question about the whole class

content.text:
If you ask your classmates about their favourite colours, you will get a list of colours. This list is an example of data. Similarly, if you measure the weight of each student in your class, you would get a collection of measures of weight, again data.
Any collection of facts, numbers, measures, observations or other descriptions of things that convey information about those things is called data.

I am not sure. How can we find the most popular game in our class?

content.text:
1. Predict first: the list has 31 names with a game beside each. Can you read the most popular game straight off the list?

3. Count each group: Hockey 8, Kabaddi 6, Cricket 6, Satoliya 5, Football 4, Badminton 2.
4. The group with the highest count is Hockey, so hockey is the most popular game, not cricket.

concepts.concept_name: Half symbols, and when a pictograph is hard to draw

content.text:
Sangita decided to use one smiley to represent 10 students instead.
Since she used one smiley to show 10 students, she had a problem in showing 25 students and 35 students in the pictograph. Then, she realised she could use a half smiley to show 5 students.
What could be the problems faced in preparing such a pictograph, if the total number of students present in a class is 33 or 27? (Math Talk)
It can be more challenging to prepare a pictograph when the amount of data is large or when the frequencies are not exact multiples of the scale or key.

maths_rules: key: 1 smiley = 10 students, half smiley = 5 students
25 students = 2 x 10 + 5 = 20 + 5
35 students = 3 x 10 + 5 = 30 + 5
33 - 30 = 3 students left after 3 smileys; a half smiley shows 5, which is more than 3
27 - 20 = 7 students left after 2 smileys; 7 - 5 = 2 students left after a half smiley
only counts made of tens and fives fit exactly
